    Dual-fuel generators offer the flexibility to run on either gasoline or propane, making them a versatile option for backup power. But with so many available, and many costing over $1,000, we tested a range of top models to help you find the right fit. Based on our results, we chose the Westinghouse WGen9500DF as our top pick for its powerful output, multiple starting options, and wide selection of outlets.

    Industry observers note that if you’re considering a dual-fuel generator but aren’t sure how much power you need or which features matter most, this guide can help. Below, we explain what to look for and share how five of the best dual-fuel generators performed in our hands-on tests.

    Industry observers note that bottom line: Dual-fuel generators offer flexibility and power for home and outdoor use. Our tests highlight the best models to suit various needs and budgets.

    It has been revealed that multifuel generators use gasoline or propane to provide electric power to your home, campground, or jobsite. But before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider whether it will meet your needs.

    Industry observers note that one key aspect of dual-fuel generators is you cannot run them indoors since they produce toxic fumes. Instead, you must set them up outside in a sheltered location and provide electrical power to appliances through an extension cord.

    They are relatively heavy, weighing 100 to 200 pounds on average, and typically loud, sometimes exceeding the acceptable volumes allowed at RV parks. An inverter generator may be a better choice if you want a quiet generator. These generators have an enclosed body and supply power using a computer-controlled inverter instead of a noisier alternator.

    However, if you need a decent amount of power, can see yourself regularly using more than one fuel type, and can handle a little extra weight and noise, a dual-fuel generator may be right for you.

    Sources indicate that the following dual-fuel generators represent the best the market has to offer in various categories. BobVila.com team members thoroughly tested each one, and we detail their pros and cons below.

    Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4.5/5.

This powerful generator runs on gasoline or propane, and selecting one or the other is as simple as flipping a switch. The WGen9500DF comes with a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will power the unit for up to 12 hours at a 25 percent load.

    Actual runtime will depend on gasoline quality and how much power you’re drawing. On propane, it can run up to 7 hours on a 20-pound tank when drawing a 50 percent load. This model has a 120/240V-50A outlet, a 120/240V-30A locking outlet, and four 120V-20A GFCI outlets. At 9,500 running watts on gasoline, it’s powerful enough to run several tools simultaneously as well as an oven/range combo and clothes dryer separately.

    Recent findings suggest that the downsides? At 211 pounds, this is a heavy generator. It’s also loud, comparable to a motorcycle, which is enough to annoy neighbors yet reasonable for its output. If you’re looking for a quiet model to use during a power outage, this might not be it. It is, however, a powerhouse of electrical output using whichever fuel is preferred.

    According to recent reports, before selecting several high-quality models for hands-on testing, we researched more than 24 dual-fuel generators, looking for quality construction, ease of use, portability, and power output. We gave some consideration to top manufacturers but didn’t automatically eliminate smaller or niche manufacturers if their generators were highly rated and competitively priced.

    For actual testing, we assembled the generators and ran them according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We allotted time to models requiring break-in periods so the machines’ internal components could lubricate and settle before powering appliances or tools. Our team of testers then plugged in power tools, appliances, and more while using an online wattage calculator to estimate a suitable electrical load.

    We awarded points to each model using a rubric considering ease of use, noise, portability, power, and value. The better a generator performed a test, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to determine top performers.

    To find the best dual-fuel generator for your home, campground, or worksite, consider the factors listed below, including fuel efficiency, fuel tank capacity, power output, and control panel configuration.

    According to recent reports, dual-fuel generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the fuel tank on the generator, the longer the generator can provide gasoline-based power. But, as tank size increases, so does the size of the generator.

    Fuel capacity does not affect how much propane you can use with your dual-fuel generator. Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

    According to recent reports, the power output on dual-fuel generators is measured in watts. Manufacturers’ specs include peak power output and running power output. Peak power output refers to the maximum number of watts the generator can provide at any one time. Running power output equals the average number of watts produced during use.

    In a recent development, dual-fuel generators generally produce a power output from 1,000 watts to over 12,000 watts, depending on their size. Gasoline produces a higher wattage than propane, so many manufacturers of dual-fuel technology break wattage into propane peak and running outputs and gasoline peak and running outputs.

    For greater power output needs, users may need to consider a standby generator rather than a portable dual-fuel option.

    You can start your dual-fuel generator with an electric start switch or a recoil cord.

    Sources indicate that A generator’s operating noise level is measured in decibels. To understand the range of sound produced by a generator, consider these common sounds and their equivalent operating dB level:.

    Recent findings suggest that many dual-fuel generators produce 50 to 90 dB of noise, depending on fuel type (gasoline runs louder than propane) and power output. The most common range is between 65 dB and 75 dB, comparable to the sound of normal conversation.

    The quietest dual-fuel generators combine dual-fuel technology and inverter technology to create a dual-fuel inverter generator.

    In a recent development, dual-fuel generators are typically large and heavy, with hoses or tanks that make them difficult to carry and move. Thus, some manufacturers include wheel kits for tilting the generator back and rolling it to the desired location.

    According to recent reports, you may also be able to purchase a wheel kit separately to add to your existing generator or replace an older wheel kit that doesn’t work well anymore. Either way, a wheel kit makes transporting a portable dual-fuel generator much easier.

    According to recent reports, lift hook bars are handy on jobsites, allowing workers to attach the generator to a hook-and-pulley system and raise or lower it instead of carrying it up or down stairs or ladders. In industrial settings, this feature helps raise the generator onto a walkway or platform.

    A lift hook bar will increase the generator’s weight (and likely the price), so don’t look for a generator with this feature unless you truly initiative to use it.

    Most dual-fuel generators are between 22 inches long by 22 inches wide by 22 inches high and 35 inches long by 30 inches wide by 30 inches high. They typically weigh between 100 and 250 pounds.

    It has been revealed that if you plan to move the generator frequently, figure size and weight prominently into your decision. Make sure the model you choose fits into your vehicle so you can transport it as needed. Remember, however, that larger, heavier motors are also the most powerful. You’ll want to find the right balance of size, weight, and power to meet your needs.

    Gasoline and propane each have their pros and cons as fuel options. Gasoline is easier to find, but propane costs less. Propane is a better fuel source in hot summer weather, while gas burns better in the cold. A dual-fuel generator lets you choose one or the other based on immediate circumstances.

    Using both fuel sources, one after the other, greatly increases a generator’s runtime. Consumers can run to the gas station to refuel while the generator keeps providing power on propane.

    Dual-fuel generators let users:.

    Before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider the answers to the following frequently asked questions.

    It has been revealed that A dual-fuel generator operates like a single-fuel generator, except it can burn propane and gasoline to produce electrical energy. It converts mechanical energy produced by the burning fuels to force the movement of electrical charges and generate electricity.

    While some single-fuel generators can be adapted for use with natural gas, this isn’t the case with dual-fuel generators. Unless specially designed, dual-fuel generators do not run on natural gas and cannot be adapted for this purpose.

    Industry observers note that propane gas is less expensive than gasoline, nearly impossible to spill, and burns cleaner, resulting in less wear on the engine over time. Running a dual-fuel generator on propane will save money but slightly decrease the machine’s peak and running watts.

    It has been revealed that runtime is determined by fuel efficiency and fuel tank capacity. On average, a standard dual-fuel generator runs about 8 to 10 hours on propane.

    If power is the goal, then the DuroMax dual-fuel generator is one of the best options to help ensure the campsite or essential home appliances have power for hours.

    Depending on how much wattage a home draws under normal situations, attaching a high-capacity dual-fuel generator to its electrical system may be possible, but it’s not a DIY project.An electrician must install a transfer switch connecting the generator to the home’s electrical main. When the power goes out, the transfer switch automatically switches the incoming power from the grid to the generator. In most cases, the generator will be classified as a “standby generator” because it’s always ready to start generating electricity. Most portable generators are too small to run an entire home.

    Generators running on gasoline are typically louder than those running on propane since burning propane requires less energy.

    As with most outdoor tools and large household appliances, you will want to take dual-fuel generators to a local recycling plant for recycling.

    Justices Thomas and Alito on State Requirements That Continuing Professional Education Discuss Certain Topics

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v.
    • According to recent reports, in 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes.
    • I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's dissent from denial of certiorari today in Khatibi v. Yip, joined by Justice Alito (Justice Gorsuch voted to grant the petition, but didn't sign on to the dissent):.

    According to recent reports, in 2022, California began requiring private instructors in privately run and privately accredited continuing medical education (CME) courses to discuss how so-called implicit bias affects healthcare outcomes. The Ninth Circuit held that First Amendment scrutiny did not apply to this compelled-speech requirement because the breadth of California's CME regulation renders the content of any CME course government speech, not private speech. That logic fundamentally misunderstands this Court's precedents and the Constitution. First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.

    I would have granted certiorari to clarify the government-speech doctrine. At a minimum, the Ninth Circuit misapplied Shurtleff v. Boston (2022), which instructs courts to identify government speech by considering (1) "the history of the expression at matter," (2) "the public's likely perception as to who (the government or a private person) is speaking," and (3) "the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression." The Ninth Circuit collapsed those distinct inquiries, focusing on the breadth of the government's regulatory scheme at each step. More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray.

    I joined Justice ALITO's concurrence in Shurtleff, which warned that the majority's three-factor test could cause courts to conclude that extensive government regulation transforms a private message into government speech exempt from First Amendment scrutiny. As the Ninth Circuit's decision shows, those concerns were prescient. This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech….

    According to recent reports, california-licensed physicians are required to complete 50 hours of approved CME every two years. Credit-eligible CME courses are often organized by private entities, certified by private accreditors, and taught by private instructors. The State does not preapprove course content but reserves the right to audit courses for compliance with its CME standards.

    The Medical Board of California "adopt[s] and administer[s] [CME] standards," few of which relate to course content. In addition, the State requires that CME courses broadly relate to the medical profession. They must "serve to maintain, develop, or increase the knowledge, skills, and professional performance that a physician and surgeon uses to provide care, or to improve the quality of care provided to patients." In 2019, however, the California Legislature added a requirement that after January 1, 2022, all CME courses must "contain curriculum that includes the understanding of implicit bias." To satisfy that requirement, CME courses must contain "[e]xamples of how implicit bias affects perceptions and treatment decisions of physicians and surgeons, leading to disparities in health outcomes" or "[s]trategies to address how unintended biases in decisionmaking may contribute to health care disparities.".

    Industry observers note that petitioners Dr. Azadeh Khatibi and Do No Harm do not want to speak California's preferred message on implicit bias, and they challenged § 2190.1(d) as compelling speech in violation of the First Amendment. Dr. Khatibi, a California-licensed ophthalmologist, creates and teaches CME courses. She "disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare" and does not want to devote time to the subject during her courses. Do No Harm is a nonprofit corporation. At least one of its members teaches CME courses and believes that implicit bias trainings "have not been shown to successfully reduce barriers to healthcare, and instead risk infecting healthcare decisions with divisive and discriminatory ideas." Yet, California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes "disparities in health outcomes…..

    The Ninth Circuit held that all three Shurtleff factors indicate that "CMEs eligible for Board credit constitute government speech." At every step of the analysis, the Ninth Circuit emphasized the breadth of the State's regulation. Considering history, the court noted that California "has long regulated the practice of medicine as an exercise of the police power" and has "adopted, updated, and enforced CME standards." Considering the public's likely perception of the speaker in a CME course, the court reasoned that "licensees could attribute approved CMEs' content to California" because "their profession is heavily regulated." Considering the extent to which the government has shaped the expression, the court cited "California's extraordinary control over accredited CMEs." As Judge VanDyke explained in his dissent from the denial of rehearing en banc, the panel's "approach boil[ed] down to a single-factor analysis: does the government 'heavily' or 'actively' regulate CMEs?" ….

    In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is "speak[ing] for itself or … regulat[ing] private expression.".

    It has been revealed that the government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people's right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself. "But courts must be very careful when a government claims that speech by one or more private speakers is actually government speech." "If private speech could be passed off as government speech by simply affixing a government seal of approval, government could … muffle the expression of disfavored viewpoints," or, as here, require private speakers to convey government messages without facing any constitutional scrutiny.

    This Court has thus exercised "great caution" before characterizing a message as government speech. In Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Assn (2005), we held that government-sponsored beef ads constituted government speech because the government determined "the overarching message" of the ads, helped develop proposals for the ads, reviewed every ad "for substance and for wording," and the Secretary of Agriculture "exercise[d] final approval authority over every word used in every" ad. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009), we held that the permanent display of monuments in a public park was government speech because the City "effectively controlled the messages sent by the monuments in the Park by exercising final approval authority over their selection." And, in Walker v. Texas Div., Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015), we held that the messages on government-issued license plates, over which the State "maintain[ed] direct control," were government speech.

    Since Walker—which we have described as the "outer boun[d] of the government-speech doctrine," Matal v. Tam (2017)—we have been careful to distinguish between government control over messages and government control over the broader scheme through which the messages are communicated. We held, for example, that trademarks are private speech, notwithstanding the government's substantial involvement in the registration process. And, this Court held that flags flown outside of Boston's City Hall did not constitute government speech in part because the city regularly permitted private groups to freely fly their own colors. In all these cases, the controlling question was whether "the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression.".

    Put in those simple terms, and in light of our precedents, California's attempt to require private individuals in privately accredited CME courses to run implicit-bias training is an evident attempt "to regulate private expression." … First, California has not historically used CME to communicate government messages. While the State requires that CME courses generally relate to the practice of medicine and occasionally requires that courses cover certain subjects, California has not otherwise dictated the content of courses.

    Recent findings suggest that second, because California "relie[s] on the participation of private parties in executing the CME scheme," the public is unlikely to perceive a private instructor's CME course as government speech. As the Ninth Circuit acknowledged, Dr. Khatibi "plausibly alleged facts suggesting that attendees treat her as the person responsible for CME content.".

    Recent findings suggest that third, while California extensively regulates the medical field, licenses physicians, and sets the requirements for credit-eligible CME, there is little evidence that California "shape[s] the messages" communicated in CME courses. Despite its long recitation of California regulations, the Ninth Circuit did not identify any state law that requires private speakers in a CME course to express a particular viewpoint—even on contestable medical problems. The implicit-bias-training requirement is a notable departure from that practice. It should have been easy, then, for the courts below to conclude that California's implicit-bias-training requirement regulates private speech.

    It has been revealed that more troubling than the Ninth Circuit's misapplication of the Shurtleff factors are the implications of the court's decision. On the Ninth Circuit's view of government speech, could California require a CME instructor to communicate the State's preferred message on the availability of abortion? Could the State require a CME instructor to inform participants that for certain patients, gender-transition surgery is ethically required?

    What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring? Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution….

    If the Ninth Circuit's decision is truly the kind of result that Shurtleff's three-factor test countenances, we should reconsider Shurtleff. Before Shurtleff, this Court had identified history, public perception, and government control as "relevant" but not mandatory "considerations" for identifying government speech. When Shurtleff described those considerations as a three-factor test, several Members of the Court—myself included—warned that the test would be unworkable and obscure the central inquiry in government-speech cases: whether the government is speaking or regulating private speech. "[L]ike any factorized analysis," the Shurtleff majority's approach does not "provide a principled way of deciding cases." Worse, myopic focus on the history and scope of government control over speech may give courts the false impression that state regulation can convert private speech into government speech.

    Industry observers note that after only a few years, those concerns are materializing. The Ninth Circuit relied on California's regulation of CME to conclude that requiring private speakers to communicate a government message was not compelled speech but government speech. That is precisely the paradox predicted by the concurrence in Shurtleff: that "government action that regulates private speech would" now "qualify as government speech unregulated by the First Amendment." But, neither compelled speech nor "[c]ensorship" are "made constitutional by aggressive and direct application." It cannot be the case that compelled speech becomes government speech because the government has compelled the speech.

    In a recent development, I would grant certiorari to correct course. In my view, the relevant inquiry in a government-speech case is straightforward: Is the government "speaking," or is it "regulating private expression"? The challenged government activity must be "government speech in the literal sense—purposeful communication of a governmentally determined message by a person acting within the scope of a power to speak for the government." Moreover, "the government must … not rely on a means that abridges the speech of persons acting in a private capacity," because doing so reveals that the government has moved from the role of speaker to that of regulator.

    Sources indicate that under this framework, it is easy to see why California's law is subject to First Amendment scrutiny. The State's implicit-bias-training requirement is not speech by any government actor; it is a requirement that private speakers communicate certain messages. Although the government may "deputiz[e] private persons as its agents" to convey its message, Dr. Khatibi and Do No Harm's members have not "voluntarily assumed" "a public or quasi-public capacity that empowers them to speak on behalf of the government." They share their own messages through the CME courses they create and deliver, and they do so in their private capacities. Even "government speech in the literal sense is not exempt from First Amendment attack if it uses a means that restricts private expression," such as "compelled speech." When, as here, the government does not concern its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies….

    A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as "a cover for censorship" or a cloak for compelled speech.

    Recent findings suggest that solar-powered Christmas lights are less common but are still a viable option. They’re an energy saver, generating energy via a solar panel during the day, but they aren’t without their flaws. The biggest problem is power consistency. Solar power must be stored to keep the lights running after the sun goes down. Many of these lights shine brightly for about 1 or 2 hours but then dim as power fades. Yes, they save power, but they’re not nearly as bright or consistent as electric lights.

    It has been revealed that LED Christmas light bulbs use light-emitting diodes instead of filaments like incandescent bulbs. The diodes require less energy and last longer than filaments, creating a long-lasting, energy-efficient light bulb. LED lights also remain cool to the touch, reducing the risk of fire. Outdoor LED Christmas lights come in a wider variety of colors than incandescent ones. When paired with smart features, they can create a rainbow of options.

    Even if you’ve been helping with outdoor Christmas lights since you were a kid, you might still have a few questions about this particular category of string lights. Our answers to the following frequently asked questions can help you get your lights selected and installed so that your home looks its best this holiday season.

    When hanging outdoor Christmas lights, recruit a helper, get a sturdy ladder, and prepare for at least a few hours of work. Start with a string near an electrical outlet and hang your Christmas lights by following the roofline. Have your helper hold the ladder for stability. If the lights you’re hanging don’t have clips, you can attach them with nails, a staple gun, or removable light clips. Of these options, the removable clips are easiest and cause the least damage to the home.

    Unlike indoor Christmas lights, outdoor Christmas lights should be 100 percent waterproof. If they’re not, they could short out the first time it rains or snows. Check the IP rating, which consists of two digits. The first number indicates dust and debris resistance, and the second indicates water resistance on a scale of 0 to 9. Waterproof outdoor Christmas lights should have a rating of at least 4 (in the second digit) or higher. Lights with a 4 or 5 can resist light rain, though they may not do well in extremely wet weather.

    Industry observers note that yes, Christmas outdoor lights are safe to leave on all night. However, you might want to connect them to a timer to save energy.

    Yes, LED outdoor Christmas lights last longer than older-style bulbs. The U.S. Department of Energy states that LED bulbs last up to 25 times longer than incandescent bulbs.

    The size of bulbs you choose for your outdoor Christmas lights depends mostly on your personal preferences. In our tests, we really liked the look of Noma’s C9 Christmas Lights on our roofline and mini lights like the Prextex White Wire Lights wrapped around our covered porch’s beams.

    Some outdoor lighting will have a control box near its plug that isn’t waterproof and must be covered or otherwise kept out of the elements. Other options for outdoor Christmas lights will be fully waterproof, as stated on the packaging.

    Choosing the best color for outdoor Christmas lights is 100 percent personal preference, so pick whichever color or colors you prefer! If you’re looking to change colors this year and want to responsibly part ways with old lights, see our guide on recycling Christmas lights for more information.

    Like color and size, brightness for outdoor Christmas lights mostly comes down to personal preference. Cool white lights may be best for you if you prefer something on the brighter end of the spectrum. Colored or warm white options typically aren’t quite as bright.

    #55864. Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

    Justice Thomas on the Second Amendment in "Sensitive Places"

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v.
    • Sources indicate that maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places.
    • According to recent reports, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that from Justice Thomas's statement respecting the denial of certiorari in Novotny v. Moore:.

    Sources indicate that maryland is one of several States that prohibit law-abiding gun owners from carrying firearms in a wide variety of public places. Under Maryland law, an individual may not carry a firearm in public demonstrations, mass transit, places of amusement, healthcare facilities, locations that sell alcohol for onsite consumption, and tens of thousands of acres of state park and forest land. The Fourth Circuit upheld these restrictions against petitioners' Second Amendment challenge because it concluded that each law banned firearms in a "sensitive place.".

    According to recent reports, I am skeptical that each of these laws "is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" in "sensitive places." Still, I agree with the Court's decision not to grant certiorari. Because each Maryland statute implicates a distinct historical tradition of firearm regulation, the breadth of petitioners' challenge would complicate our review. In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however, we should consider the scope of States' authority to ban firearms in "sensitive places.".

    It has been revealed that the Second Amendment recognizes the people's "inherent" right to keep and bear firearms, a right that admits of only historically grounded exceptions. Before and after the founding, it was well understood that individuals enjoyed a natural right to keep and bear arms, which included the right to carry firearms in public spaces for self-defense. The Constitution "codified [that] pre-existing right." The first generations after the founding recognized the breadth of the Second Amendment's "guarante[e]," and "those who sought to carry firearms publicly and peaceably in antebellum America were generally free to do so." Thus, when a State seeks to restrict the right to bear arms—including by limiting the places in which a law-abiding citizen may carry his firearm—the State must root its law in the Second Amendment's "historical understanding" by "demonstrat[ing] that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation.".

    This Court has previously acknowledged a limited tradition of States' regulating the right to carry firearms in certain "sensitive places." In Bruen, we observed that early American legislatures sometimes prohibited weapons in "legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses." But, we emphasized that this tradition was narrow. "[T]he historical record yields relatively few 18th- and 19th-century 'sensitive places' where weapons were altogether prohibited." While "courts can use analogies to those historical regulations of 'sensitive places' to determine that modern regulations … are constitutionally permissible," "expanding the category of 'sensitive places' … to all places of public congregation … would eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense.".

    Nevertheless, States have seized on the idea of "sensitive places" to prohibit the peaceable carry of firearms in locations that bear little resemblance to legislatures, polling places, or courthouses. New Jersey, for example, prohibits firearms in at least 25 locations, including zoos, public libraries, casinos, and state-owned beaches. New York has designated 20 locations as "sensitive," ranging from "any place of worship" to "residential settings licensed … by the department of health." California's 29 gun-free spaces include "athletic facilit[ies]," "financial institution[s]," and any government-permitted "public gathering or special event." {Several other States ban firearms in many public places.} These restrictions stand on questionable historical ground. And, their cumulative effect is to prohibit firearms wherever people gather for eating, drinking, recreation, amusement, and free speech—an affront to the right of "law-abiding citizens" to "carr[y] arms in public for" their "ordinary self-defense.".

    The lower courts have largely blessed these ahistorical ventures. The Fourth Circuit below upheld all but one of Maryland's locational restrictions. A now-vacated decision of the Third Circuit upheld many of Latest Jersey's "sensitive-place" laws. Courts of Appeals have also rejected challenges to specific locational restrictions in New York, California, and Hawaii.

    According to recent reports, I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions. In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry.

    The 10 Best Ways to Use Your Grandma’s Favorite $5 Cleaner

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • As a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous.
    • Before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    As a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous. But in its diluted household form, the nitrogen-based super cleaner is a workhorse in the war on common household dirt and grime. Ammonia is readily available, inexpensive, and potent, so a little goes a long way.

    Before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from. You may see “cloudy” or “sudsy” versions—that’s ammonia with soap added, which is generally used for such domestic cleaning chores as treating stained clothing or scrubbing stovetops. We recommend opting for “clear” ammonia, which is suited to a wider variety of tasks (and you can always add a tablespoon or two of dish soap to make clear ammonia sudsy). You’ll also find ammonia that’s scented with lemon or pine to temper its stinging odor.

    It has been revealed that the harsh smell serves as a warning, though: Working with ammonia absolutely requires caution. Pure chemical ammonia can cause severe burns and respiratory issues if it comes into contact with skin or is ingested. Even diluted in water, as is recommended for most cleaning purposes, ammonia can still be harmful.

    Mixing ammonia and chlorine bleach creates a toxic gas called chloramine. Take great care not to combine them—doing so could have dire consequences.

    The most vital safety rule to remember is: Never mix ammonia with chlorine bleach. The result is a highly toxic chlorine gas that can produce headaches, seizures, and other symptoms. It’s crucial to keep this in mind if you’re using ammonia with laundry or to clean surfaces. You want to make absolutely sure not to mix it with a detergent or household cleaner that contains bleach.

    When using ammonia, be sure to wear chemical-resistant gloves and ventilate the area well. Be sure, too, to store it where pets and children can’t access it. Bearing these safety guidelines in mind, put ammonia to work around the home, as generations have done before us.

    To achieve streak-free mirrors, windows, and crystal, mix 1 tablespoon clear ammonia with 2 cups water in a spray bottle. Spritz the solution onto glass items and wipe immediately with a soft, lint-free cloth for windows and crystal; paper towels work fine for mirrors.

    To remove stains on a concrete driveway, garage floor, or patio, mix 1 cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and apply it to the stain with a mop or large sponge. Let sit for about 20 minutes, and then scrub the stain with a bristled brush. Rinse the surface with clean water. If the stain isn’t completely gone after the area dries, repeat the process until you’re satisfied with the results.

    Sources indicate that if gold, silver, diamond, or platinum jewelry has lost its shine, mix 6 parts warm water to 1 part ammonia in a bowl (one that you don’t eat or cook with and add your jewelry. (Never use ammonia to clean pearls or other gems.) After 15 minutes, remove the jewelry with your gloved hand, and then gently scrape away any stubborn grime with a soft-bristled toothbrush (one that’s no longer in use or designated for cleaning). Allow it to soak for another 15 minutes, remove from the solution, and immediately rinse with warm water. Dispose of used ammonia solution down the drain while running the hot water. Polish the jewelry with a soft, lint-free cloth and let it dry.

    Stubborn stains on cotton, polyester, or nylon fabrics are no match for a solution of ⅔ cup clear ammonia, ⅔ cup dish soap, 6 tablespoons of baking soda, and 2 cups warm water. Mix in a bowl or bucket and apply generously to stains with a sponge or spray bottle. Let the treatment sit for about 30 minutes, then launder as usual. For tougher stains like blood or grass, treat the stain again with a solution of 1 part ammonia and 1 part warm water.

    Industry observers note that note: Do not use ammonia on wool or silk, which can eat through the delicate fabrics. And remember never to mix ammonia with any laundry products that contain bleach.

    Recent findings suggest that tackle caked-on grease on stove burners with this trick. Place each burner in a separate sealable plastic bag filled with ¼ cup ammonia. Seal each bag to keep fumes at bay, and place in a sink or washtub for 8 to 12 hours. Open the bags in a ventilated area, and remove all grease and dirt easily with a quick scrub of dish soap and water. Once the gunk is gone, thoroughly rinse the burners with water to get rid of ammonia residue. Let dry completely before using.

    Recent findings suggest that mix one part clear ammonia and one part hot water in a sprayer or other bottle. Apply generously to the stain by spritzing or with a sponge. After about 10 minutes of dwell time, place a clean old towel over the stain and press with an iron, blasting with steam, for about 20 seconds. Check your progress: The stain should start transferring to the towel. Repeat, with steam ironing and more ammonia solution if needed, until the stain is gone.

    Ammonia is tough on every odor from fresh paint to burnt lasagna. Place a small container filled with about 1/2 cup of clear ammonia near an offending smell, being sure to keep the area ventilated, to absorb the nastiness within hours.

    According to recent reports, heat the oven to 150 degrees, and set a large pot of water on the stove to boil. Turn off the oven and open the windows to ventilate the kitchen. Place a sturdy container, such as a glass measuring cup or metal bowl, filled with ½ cup ammonia on the oven’s top shelf. Place the pot of boiled water on the bottom shelf. Close the oven and let sit for 8 to 12 hours, then remove the containers of ammonia and water. Open the oven door and air air out for at least an hour before cleaning. Because the grime has basked in ammonia fumes, it should be loosened and easy to remove with a sponge, warm water, and dish soap.

    This method is only recommended for electric ovens, because mixing ammonia with gas can be dangerous. If you choose to use this method on your gas oven, make sure that the pilot light and gas lines are turned off.

    To clean and disinfect kitchen and bath tiles, mix ¼ cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and use a sponge or mop to liberally apply the solution to the tile. Use a soft-bristled brush to scrub any particularly stubborn areas. Finish up by rinsing the surface with clean water and your sponge or mop.

    According to recent reports, ammonia’s strong scent can deter unwanted critters. Fill a saucer with clear, unscented ammonia, or saturate a rag or cotton balls with it. Then place in areas that attract pests, such as near garbage cans where raccoons prowl or beside cracks in the basement where mice enter. The smell will remind the varmints of predators, so they’re likely to catch a whiff and turn away, unharmed. That said, make sure to keep the ammonia deterrent out of reach of kids and pets.

So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up.     Not only are wood stoves a reliable heat source for homes, cabins, and even tents, but they also create a rustic feel and cozy ambience. Since they come in a range of styles and sizes—from standalone models and fireplace inserts to portable camping stoves—choosing the right one means considering the size of your space, the stove’s heat output, and how you’ll use it.

    To build this guide, we researched more than 20 of the most popular wood stoves. Based on our efforts, we chose the Ashley Hearth 2,000-Sq-Ft Wood Stove With Pedestal as the best overall for its substantial heating capacity, durable construction, and easy-clean ash pan. We also found options we like for smaller spaces, cooking at camp, and more, so you can find the best wood stove for your needs.

    Bottom line: Explore the best wood stoves of 2026, featuring top picks for various needs and budgets, from efficient home heating to portable camping solutions.

    Industry observers note that the list below takes into account our shopping considerations to feature the best wood-burning stove models on the market. It includes stand-alone models and indoor wood-burning fireplace stove inserts, as well as portable wood stoves for outdoor use.

    It has been revealed that with its impressive 89,000 BTU heat output, this wood-burning stove from Ashley Hearth is an excellent choice for warming larger living spaces. The plate-steel body has a firebrick-lined interior that improves combustion efficiency and durability, a cast-iron door that adds a traditional touch, and an air-washed ceramic glass window that makes it easy to see the flames. The noncatalytic secondary combustion system burns wood without a catalytic combustor, and the stove doesn’t require any electricity to use, which is essential if the power goes out.

    Beyond those aspects, there are several other practical details that earned this model the top spot. First, the firebox can accommodate logs up to 21 inches long, meaning you won’t spend half your night cutting all your wood into small enough pieces, and second, the removable ash pan and built-in ash port make routine cleanup easy. Plus, the pedestal base gives the whole thing a finished, furniture-like appearance. The only real downside is that the blower Ashley recommends is sold separately and requires electricity, so you’ll want to factor that into overall cost and convenience before buying.

    Get the Ashley Hearth 2,000-square-foot wood stove at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

    With its classic appearance and high heat output, this wood-burning stove from US Stove is a worthy choice for warming the home. It consists of a cast-iron body with a modern U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-certified interior suitable for clean burning. The slim design can fit snugly in most homes taking minimal space while effectively heating areas of up to 900 square feet with its 54,000 BTUs.

    Industry observers note that this cast-iron wood stove also includes an integrated cooking surface on the top of the unit, ideal for preparing small meals. The deceptively small interior can accept wood of up to 19 inches in length.

    Get the US Stove wood stove at Ace Hardware or The Home Depot.

    Industry observers note that while this stove from Woodstock Soapstone costs twice as much as or more than other wood stoves, its ability to burn cleanly while producing an exceptional amount of heat makes it one of the top-performing models available. As a catalytic stove, it produces low emissions of just 0.63 grams per hour while delivering up to 47,220 BTUs of heat—enough to warm homes of 2,200 square feet or larger.

    This high-efficiency wood stove is designed to burn for 14 hours or more on a single load of wood. Its white-and-black marbled soapstone exterior and vintage cast-iron molded frame also provide visual appeal, with four other color options to choose from. The large front window provides an excellent view of the flames, which are enclosed by a 7-gauge-thick welded firebox.

    Get the Woodstock Soapstone wood stove at Woodstock Soapstone.

    According to recent reports, A compact size and high BTU output make this Ashley Hearth model from US Stove one of the best wood stove inserts on the market. With its 69,000-BTU output, it’s capable of heating up to 1,200 square feet. It’s made from 4.76-millimeter-thick plate steel with firebrick lining on the interior. The 16.5-inch-by-9-inch door is made from cast iron and comes with a ceramic glass window, which provides a wide view of the flames.

    In a recent development, the stove is large enough to burn logs up to 18 inches long and has a 65.5 percent efficiency rating. A blower on the bottom of the insert helps circulate warm air through the room. The entire heater measures 20.1875 inches long by 26.5 inches wide by 22.375 inches high and has a spring-loaded automatic adjuster that makes it easier to install into a wall.

    Get the Ashley Hearth wood stove insert at Wayfair or Woodstovepro.

    It has been revealed that this large, well-designed wood stove from Winnerwell is ideal for cooking with wood while camping. At 108 inches long by 25 inches wide by 20 inches deep and weighing 34 pounds, this stainless steel stove is compact enough for taking to the campground to heat a tent, yurt, or tepee. It’s made from stainless steel to resist rust and corrosion from rain. It includes five sections of 3.5-inch-diameter chimney pipe that attach to the exhaust pipe at the top of the stove for venting smoke to the exterior of the tent or structure.

    It has been revealed that the flat top is large enough to support a pot for boiling water or a pan for frying up eggs. Two grates fold out and serve as side racks for cooking. The firebox is accessible via windowed doors on the front and side of the stove.

    Get the Winnerwell wood stove at Amazon or Winnerwell.

    Most wood stoves require a substantial chunk of space. This Ashley Hearth model from US Stove comes in at just under 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep—a much smaller footprint, making it ideal for heating tinier rooms and homes. Despite its compact size, it still puts out enough heat to warm a 1,200-square-foot room.

    According to recent reports, the stove consists of plated-steel construction with a cast-iron door that features a large glass window to provide a nice view of the burning logs. Despite its small size, the door is wide enough to handle logs up to 18 inches long. A brushed-nickel handle on the loading door and ash drawers add an elegant look to this rustic wood stove.

    Get the Ashley Hearth 1,200-square-foot wood stove at Lowe’s.

    We considered numerous criteria when narrowing the field of wood stoves to these top selections. A wood stove’s ability to produce heat is key, so we only considered models that could provide heat for 900 square feet of space or more (except for the portable and camping categories).

    Since the visible flames are a large part of a wood stove’s appeal, we mainly selected models that provide a good view of the firebox with large windows on the doors. Build quality is crucial, so we only chose models with higher-gauge steel construction and forged-iron doors, except for our upgrade pick, which uses soapstone.

    Understanding the two types of wood stoves, the materials used to make them, and their heating capacity are all vital when shopping for one of these appliances. Ahead, learn more about these and other important attributes of the best wood stoves.

    Wood stoves are available in two types: catalytic and noncatalytic. Catalytic wood stoves differ from noncatalytic in that they produce fewer exhaust fumes and burn more efficiently. In addition to burning wood, catalytic wood stoves also have a combustor that burns smoke and byproducts. This design allows the stove to burn cleaner with a slower burn rate, conserving fuel. Efficiency ratings for a catalytic wood stove range between 63 and 84 percent, making them ideal options for use as a primary source of heat.

    According to recent reports, noncatalytic stoves are cheaper but not as efficient. They are better suited for use as a supplemental heater.

    Most wood stoves are made from one of three materials: cast iron, plate steel, or soapstone. Cast iron, the most commonly used material, heats up quickly and retains warmth longer than other materials. However, it does crack more easily and is more expensive than other materials.

    It has been revealed that plate steel, also a common material used in wood stoves, is durable and retains heat well, though not as well as cast iron. Soapstone is a high-end material for wood stoves. It retains heat better than cast iron, burns cleaner than other materials, and can burn for 24 hours or longer on a single load. Most wood stoves consist of either soapstone or plate steel with a cast-iron door.

    It has been revealed that A wood stove’s heating capacity determines how large of a space the wood stove can keep warm when it’s running with a full load of wood. The heating area for most stoves ranges from around 1,200 square feet for a small stove to as much as 2,200 square feet (or more) for a large model.

    Keep in mind that, unlike a home’s central heating, which distributes heat through ductwork, a wood stove emanates heat from the fire, so the heat isn’t evenly distributed. The farther someone is from the wood stove, the cooler the temperature will be.

    Industry observers note that the heat output of a wood stove is measured in BTUs (British thermal units). Wood stoves range in BTU output from around 50,000 to 80,000 BTUs. The more BTUs, the greater the size of the space the wood stove can heat. A large 70,000-BTU wood stove can warm up to 2,200 square feet. While BTU level is a great indication of how powerful the stove is, not all manufacturers provide BTU information for their stoves.

    Recent findings suggest that A wood stove’s burn time is the amount of time one load of wood lasts before the stove requires reloading. Each stove’s burn time is determined by how much wood it can hold as well as the heat output of the stove, which can be regulated using the stove’s damper. The firewood type being used also affects burn time. Hardwoods burn more efficiently than softwood, which is less dense and therefore burns more promptly and at lower temperatures.

    Industry observers note that wood-burning stoves produce toxic emissions; they create carbon monoxide, which can be deadly if not properly vented outside. Wood stoves are regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency, which performs safety tests on wood stoves to make sure they’re safe for consumer use. The emission limit for wood stoves is 2 grams to 2.5 grams per hour, depending on the type of wood. Catalytic stoves produce well under the EPA’s maximum, with emissions of around 0.5 grams per hour. Never buy a wood stove that is not certified by the EPA.

    Perhaps the most vital thing to consider when shopping for a wood stove is where it will go in the living space. Most freestanding wood stoves take up a significant chunk of real estate since they measure about 3 feet wide and 2 feet deep and require a buffer around them for safety. Portable models are much smaller—about 20 inches high and 10 inches deep and less than 40 pounds—allowing them to fit in the trunk of a car for a camping trip.

    Industry observers note that keep in mind that the size of the stove also affects the size of wood they can burn. A standard freestanding or insert wood stove can hold logs up to 18 inches long, whereas portable models can typically handle logs that measure about 8 inches long.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to providing a source of heat, wood stoves also create an ambience that’s similar to a wood-burning fireplace. Most wood stoves have glass windows that allow people sitting around the stove to watch the burning logs.

    Some wood stoves also serve as a cooking stove, with flat tops that will support a frying pan or pot. Stoves with cooking functions are typically designed for outdoor use and camping trips.

    The best place for a wood stove is as close to the center of the area requiring heat as possible. This allows the stove to radiate warmth in all directions, better heating the space.

    Recent findings suggest that hardwoods—which include oak, maple, ash, and birch—are the best-burning woods. They will burn longer and hotter than softwoods like pine and also contain the least amount of pitch and sap inside of them.

    It has been revealed that use a brush to sweep up any debris or ash that was not collected by the fireplace’s ash pan. Next, use a wire brush to clean off any buildup inside the flue pipe. Wipe off the exterior of the wood stove with a dry cloth. Be sure to avoid using liquids, which can leave streaks.

    The average wood stove should last between 10 and 20 years, depending on usage and care.

    It is safe to leave a wood fireplace on overnight, as long as you follow a few precautions. Allow the wood to burn for a few hours before going to bed. Before turning in for the night, add ash to the burning logs to dampen the flames and slow the burning process. Next, close the stove air vents to reduce the size of the fire, ensuring it will be safe even when burning through the night.

    According to recent reports, yes. If the indoor wood-burning stove is not properly vented to the outside of the home, it can cause exhaust fumes to collect inside the home, resulting in carbon monoxide poisoning. If a wood-burning stove is installed properly, vented to the outside of the home, and EPA certified, it is safe to use.

    #55847. Court Ordered Social Media Personality to Stop Posting About Teenagers He Accused as to Nolan Wells' Death

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)

    Court Ordered Social Media Personality to Stop Posting About Teenagers He Accused as to Nolan Wells' Death

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct.
    • According to recent reports, defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders.
    • The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct. 12; the case has just been removed to federal court, which will now consider the defendant's arguments against the injunction. Here's the key passage from the injunction, a temporary restraining order that was issued before the defendant could respond:.

    Here's the heart of plaintiffs' argument:.

    According to recent reports, defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders. But it also argues (I think correctly) that is an overbroad prior restraint that violates the First Amendment:.

    The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment. It prohibits speech about the Plaintiffs, their families, and their lawyers—whether truthful or false, threatening or harmless, harassing or not. And it does so before that speech occurs. The Supreme Court has repeatedly condemned such prior restraints, particularly when imposed without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

    The Court need not decide whether Mr. Hughes's commentary was fair, tasteful, or justified. The question is whether the law permits this order. It does not. The order should be dissolved, and the motion for a preliminary injunction denied….

    A judicial order "forbidding certain communications when issued in advance of the time that such communications are to occur" is a prior restraint…. "Any system of prior restraints on communication bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." Such restraints are unconstitutional "except in exceptional circumstances." .As the Supreme Court held in Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), {the party seeking to suppress speech} "carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the imposition of such a restraint." ….

    Sources indicate that the remedy for false or injurious statements lies in "actions under libel laws providing for redress and punishment, and not in proceedings to restrain the publication." [But t]he October 12 Order … does not impose consequences for particular statements adjudicated unlawful. It prohibits Mr. Hughes from speaking about entire categories of people in the future. That is a prior restraint in its most direct form which is presumed unconstitutional….

    Industry observers note that test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh (5th Cir. 2005) … recognized that a court may enjoin "harassing communication" and "repeated invasions of privacy." But an injunction prohibiting all communication, rather than limiting itself to "threatening or harassing conduct," "swept too broadly" and constituted an unconstitutional restraint. Id.….

    Plaintiffs cannot justify the restraint merely by characterizing Mr. Hughes's commentary as malicious, coercive, or injurious. The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Keefe. There, the Court held that an individual's "interest in being free from public criticism of his business practices" did not justify an injunction against speech…. Plaintiffs may have remedies for unlawful conduct. But those remedies do not include an order forbidding Mr. Hughes from speaking about them at all….

    Defendant also argues (again correctly, I think) that the order was unconstitutional because defendant wasn't given an opportunity to be heard before the order was entered:.

    The absence of notice presents a separate constitutional defect. In Carroll v. President & Commissioners of Princess Anne (1968), the Supreme Court set aside a short ex parte order restraining expression because of "a basic infirmity in the procedure by which it was obtained." The order "was issued ex parte, without notice to petitioners and without any effort, however informal, to invite or permit their participation in the proceedings.".

    There is a place in our jurisprudence for ex parte issuance, without notice, of temporary restraining orders of short duration; There is no place within the area of basic freedoms guaranteed by the First Amendment for such orders where no showing is made that it is impossible to serve or to notify the opposing parties and to give them an opportunity to participate.

    It has been revealed that the Court also rejected the suggestion that a later hearing could cure the problem. The availability of a subsequent opportunity to be heard "does not overcome the infirmity in the absence of a showing of justification for the ex parte nature of the proceedings.".

    Sources indicate that the reason is straightforward. "The value of judicial decision-making … is substantially diluted where the process is ex parte, because the Court does not have available the fundamental instrument for judicial judgment: "an adversary proceeding in which both parties may participate." And where First Amendment freedoms are at stake, any order must be "couched in the narrowest terms that will accomplish the pin-pointed objective.".

    Industry observers note that the October 12 Order fails both principles. It was entered without notice or an adversary hearing. It contains no finding that notifying Mr. Hughes was impossible. And far from identifying a narrow category of unlawful speech, it prohibits virtually any online commentary concerning the Plaintiffs, their families, or their counsel.

    It has been revealed that carroll is directly controlling on the constitutional defect. An ex parte order restraining expression cannot stand without a showing that notice and participation were impossible. No such showing appears here….

    We liked that the attached gutter clips made them easy to hang on an overhead clothesline.     Each impact-resistant acrylic bulb that makes up these outside patio lights uses just 1 watt of power and produces a warm glow. The included remote allowed us to switch between single solid colors, two-color combinations, and various preset color modes for Christmas and Saint Patrick’s Day.

Each button-shaped LED light snaps into a base that must be screwed into the eave. It wasn’t difficult—just time-consuming.

We were able to program the lights to come on at a predetermined time. We also liked that, during the day, the lights were barely noticeable thanks to their low-profile design.

    These solar LED string lights weathered a rainstorm without any problems and then lit up the following evening. They also survived our drop test without any cracks. Then, we discovered these little decorative lights could be synced to music, and we had our own little discotheque.     According to recent reports, with or without the bronze shades, this is an attractive set of string lights for patio or porch use. It comes with 24 solid acrylic bulbs that are shatterproof and water-resistant.     In a recent development, when selecting outdoor string lighting for our tests, we promptly discovered dozens of highly rated products. We considered brand names to an extent—after all, manufacturers like Govee are highly respected in the lighting industry. We also looked at bulb type. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, opting for LED lighting instead of incandescent can save the average family more than $200 annually. We didn’t test LED lights exclusively but focused strongly on that type.

    It has been revealed that to begin our testing, we hung the string lights and left them in place for several days. After dark, we attempted to read or perform other activities—such as grilling—with just the illumination from the lights. We used a testing rubric, scoring each product based on illumination, light quality, and overall ambience. We tested every feature, including syncing the smart outdoor lights we tested with a wireless network and controlling the lights via an app.

    If the string lights were marketed as shatterproof, we dropped them on a concrete patio from head height to see if they would crack. For the ones advertised as waterproof, we left them out in a rainstorm or sprayed them with water. Then, we tested them again after they dried. We noted the cord’s length, the number of bulb sockets, and how easy they were to hang.

    Sources indicate that A simple strand of string lights can transform a plain backyard into an inviting outdoor space. Compared with many other types of exterior house lights, string lights are among the most affordable and easiest to install. If you want to hang string lights outdoors, consider light type, size and shape, brightness, and color. A weather-resistant design, a lengthy cord, and a remote or app control can make the lights safer and easier to use.

    Most outdoor string lights feature LED, incandescent, solar, or battery-operated bulbs. Each type varies in durability, energy efficiency, and lifespan. When shopping for outdoor string lights, consider which type of lighting is most suitable for the space.

    Since outdoor string lights are exposed to the elements, it’s crucial to select a set that can withstand rainy conditions and heavy gusts of wind. It’s inconvenient to take the string lights down every time inclement weather is forecast.

    First, check the product description to determine if the lights are intended for outdoor use. Using indoor lighting outside creates a potential fire hazard. Second, make sure the product is water-resistant (or waterproof, as even spots under a porch or gazebo roof can grow damp in bad weather). Weather-resistant lights can handle direct exposure to water and feature watertight seals to protect their interior components from accumulating moisture and causing safety issues.

    String light bulbs are available in a variety of styles and shapes, which can give the strands a unique aesthetic.

    According to Friedman, “You’ll also want to look for shatterproof bulbs, ideally LED, since they’re cooler and more efficient.”.

    When choosing a bulb size, consider the available outdoor space, ease of installation, and desired look.

    Small bulbs are a good pick for small outdoor spaces or garden lighting; they won’t overpower a space or other outdoor decorations. These bulbs are generally more subtle, providing gentle background lighting. They provide less light and are commonly chosen for decorative purposes.

    According to recent reports, large bulbs are more striking and offer a bolder look. Their larger size can provide more direct illumination. Generally brighter, they’re well suited to larger spaces that need more lighting. Large decorative bulbs, such as globe bulbs and Edison bulbs, can make a style statement.

    Keep in mind that bulb size can affect installation. String lights with small bulbs are generally lightweight and easier to maneuver. They may be easier to install than string lights with larger, heavier, and bulkier bulbs.

    Most globe outdoor string light bulbs come in one of three bulb sizes:.

    Most Edison-style string light bulbs are an S14 bulb size, which is a medium-size, oval-shaped bulb that’s 32 millimeters (just over 1.25 inches) in diameter.

    When it comes to the appearance of outdoor string lights, brightness and color temperature are two of the most important factors to consider.

    Lumens measure the amount of light output from a bulb—the more lumens, the brighter the bulb. When deciding on bulb brightness, take into account the desired lighting effect. String light bulbs can range from 5 to more than 100 lumens per bulb. Users often choose string lights for their glowy appearance rather than their brightness, so lower lumens often do just fine to set the mood. Lumens are different from wattage, as wattage measures how much power a bulb consumes and not necessarily how bright a light appears.

    It has been revealed that lighting color temperature is measured using the Kelvin temperature scale. This scale measures how warm or cool the light appears. Lower numbers on the Kelvin scale look warmer, and higher numbers look cooler.

    Sources indicate that most home lighting falls between 2000K and 6000K. Bulbs around 2700K have a cozy, warm white color with a yellow hue, while bulbs over 5000K offer stark, crisp lighting with a blue hue. Warm lighting makes a space look more cozy and inviting, while cool lighting can often appear harsh, especially at night. For this reason, warmer bulbs are generally preferred for ambient outdoor lighting.

    Outdoor string lights typically come in lengths of 10, 25, 35, 50, and 100 feet. When choosing the ideal wire length, consider the size of the outdoor space and the lighting layout.

    Sources indicate that patio string lights can outline garden borders, wrap around banisters and trees, or suspend over seating spaces. The best way to determine the necessary wire length is to use a piece of twine to measure where the lights will go. If the lights require corded power, make sure to include enough length to reach the outlet, or keep an extension cord handy.

    To line one side of an average balcony or small porch, a 10-foot string of outdoor patio lights may do the trick. A small 8-foot-long by 6-foot-wide patio space typically requires 25 to 50 feet of string lighting. A medium 12-foot-square outdoor space may need 50 to 100 feet of string lighting, depending on the desired layout. For more spacious areas or to illuminate a large event, more than 100 feet of string lighting is usually necessary.

    In terms of wire strength, Friedman recommends commercial-grade stringers with heavy-gauge wire. “This will hold tension much better, and the extra insulation will provide safety and durability.” He adds that “these stringers are much heavier than your average consumer string lights, so make sure you mount them securely.”.

    Sources indicate that for those who want to upgrade from basic string lights, consider a product with extra features like color-changing bulbs, dimming options, and remote control or app operation. As we discovered in our tests, users are able to create entirely different moods by selecting different bulb colors.

    According to recent reports, string lights can instantly transform a typical yard or patio into a warm and inviting space, but choosing the right set of lights is a must for creating the desired atmosphere. Still considering the best outdoor string lights for your space? Read on for answers to some frequently asked questions about selecting and installing outdoor string lights.

    White light is the most effective lighting color since it is closest to natural light. Warm white lights have a cozy, inviting yellow tinge, making them a popular pick for outdoor lighting. Colorful bulbs are often chosen for the ambience they create rather than their lighting ability. These lights add a decorative flair and can be a fun addition for different seasons and holidays.

    Industry observers note that the Lemontec Commercial-Grade Outdoor String Lights offer fifteen 11-watt incandescent bulbs and are one of the best options in the lineup for those seeking a brighter set of outdoor string lights. Plus, additional sets can be connected for even more illumination.

    Yes, some weather-resistant and weatherproof string lights can be left outdoors. Be sure to check their specifications to ensure the lights can handle changing weather and temperature conditions year-round.

    The easiest way to hang lights is to use existing fixtures or to wrap them around columns and railings surrounding a patio. If necessary, create hanging options by installing metal hooks, heavy-duty sticky hooks, or nails where needed.

    No, outdoor string lights typically use very little electricity—especially LED models, which are more energy efficient than incandescent.
